title: Article 2, the Windsor Framework and Northern Ireland: constitutional and legal concerns
label: 17 September 2026 · Article 2/Windsor Framework evidence session
summary: Jim Allister (TUV) told the committee that Article 2 of the Protocol/Windsor Framework entrenches EU-made rights in Northern Ireland without democratic consent, creating a permanent democratic and constitutional problem. He argued the provision is inseparable from the wider protocol, disenfranchises Northern Irish voters on many issues, and was conceded by UK negotiators under political pressure. On the law, he welcomed the Supreme Court's Dillon decision as narrowing Article 2's reach but warned Section 7A gives Article 2(1) direct legal effect; he said the ultimate remedy is repeal of the protocol.

chapters.title: Allister's opening: Article 2 is a democratic problem
chapters.takeaway: Allister says Article 2 ties Northern Ireland to EU-made rights without local democratic control and is inseparable from the protocol's broader loss of sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourself for the record.

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: I'm Jim Allister, MP for North Antrim and leader of the TUV. Article 2 is part of the Protocol/Windsor Framework and, I argue, it removes Northern Ireland's democratic right to make or change many laws by subjecting us to 'dynamic alignment' with EU rules.

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: We already had local rights—fair employment, equal pay, race and sex discrimination laws—made here by our elected representatives. Article 2 imposes rights from outside, on an ongoing basis, and that's a constitutional and democratic insult.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why include Article 2 in the deal? Could it have a positive purpose as a guarantee of rights?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: I think it flowed from a desperate UK negotiating position under Boris Johnson and the EU's political aim to keep influence here. Article 2 gives permanent alignment without the four-year 'consent' vote that other parts of the package have.

chapters.title: Why this matters for sovereignty and the Belfast Agreement
chapters.takeaway: Allister argues the Protocol undermined key Belfast Agreement protections, removed cross‑community safeguards, and disenfranchised Northern Irish voters on many laws.

turns.speaker: Lord Dodds of Duncairn
turns.text: Is Article 2 subject to the four‑year consent vote or any Stormont scrutiny?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: No—Article 2 is not subject to that vote. I haven't seen it scrutinised as part of the consent mechanism.

turns.speaker: Lord Dodds of Duncairn
turns.text: Is the Protocol supposed to protect the Belfast Agreement?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: That claim is nonsense. The Belfast Agreement is an independent binding agreement; it didn't need Article 2. Instead, the Protocol removed protections—most notably the cross‑community requirement—so the four‑year consent vote itself was stripped of cross‑community safeguards.

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: The Agreement also guarantees the right to pursue democratic national and political aspirations. Article 2 and the broader Protocol deny that by placing many laws beyond the reach of Northern Irish electors.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But the UK Parliament passed Section 7A, approving this—doesn't that count as democratic approval?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Parliament did pass Section 7A, but that created the very conduit that disenfranchises my constituents in over 300 areas. Parliamentary approval doesn't erase the fact Northern Ireland voters can't elect representatives to change those laws.

chapters.title: Legal limits: the Dillon judgment and court routes
chapters.takeaway: The Dillon Supreme Court decision narrows how Article 2 can be used, but Section 7A still gives Article 2(1) direct effect domestically, so legal challenges and clarifications will continue.

turns.speaker: Baroness Foster of Aghadrumsee
turns.text: What's your reading of the Dillon judgment's impact on Article 2?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Dillon narrows when Article 2 can be invoked. It applies the Demirel test—clear, precise, unconditional obligations—and ties reliance on Article 2 to specific measures listed in Annexe 1. That reins in over‑ambitious uses.

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: But Dillon also confirmed Section 7A creates direct domestic effect for Article 2(1), which is constitutionally worrying because it makes some EU‑derived rights directly enforceable here.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ludford
turns.text: Will further clarity come from more court cases or legislation?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Primarily more litigation—judicial reviews up to the Supreme Court. Some may try declaratory legislation, but Dillon already imposes legal limits.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So claimants should use the courts—the usual route?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Yes. Judicial review is the correct route to test asserted rights under Article 2, though my constitutional objection to having that route available at all remains.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about the Equality and Human Rights Commissions named in Article 2—are they acting impartially?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: By their actions they appear partisan. They have been proactive in using Article 2 to expand EU influence and have not used their powers to challenge the disenfranchisement created by the Protocol.

chapters.title: Politics, public views and remedies
chapters.takeaway: Allister says the democratic remedy is to repeal the Protocol; he rejects accepting permanent EU‑derived rights in Northern Ireland and prefers rights determined by UK institutions.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ludford
turns.text: Wasn't it foreseeable that Brexit would create special problems for Northern Ireland?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Problems could be foreseen, but the claim that the Belfast Agreement required the Irish Sea border is false. The UK chose to accept that partitioning of its internal market; it didn't flow from the Belfast Agreement.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ritchie of Downpatrick
turns.text: How should rights be protected for everyone in Northern Ireland?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: By the sovereign UK Parliament. My aim is parity with the rest of the UK: the rights we have should be those determined by UK institutions, not a separate, permanently aligned EU rights regime.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ritchie of Downpatrick
turns.text: Do you accept the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) as underpinning rights?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: I don't insist on withdrawing from the ECHR here. My point is simply that Article 2 layers in additional, externally-made rights that Northern Ireland did not democratically approve.

turns.speaker: Baroness Sanderson of Welton
turns.text: Do your constituents understand Article 2 and feel their rights are threatened?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Most won't know the legal detail, but they feel unease: being treated as if they can't elect people to change key laws, subject to checks on goods with GB, and tied to the Republic's rules in many areas.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Ballinamallard
turns.text: If asked for legal advice after Dillon, what practical steps would you recommend to meet rights obligations?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Start with sovereignty: restore the ability of Northern Ireland's elected representatives, and UK institutions, to make those laws. Practically, that means removing the Protocol in full—Article 2 is integral but not the only offending part.

turns.speaker: Lord Dodds of Duncairn
turns.text: Some argue Parliament's sovereignty allows such changes—even radical ones—and that's the constitutional mechanism at work.

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: Parliament can do many things, but here it has used its power to disenfranchise my constituents in specific areas. That's constitutionally unacceptable in a democracy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you for your evidence. Any final point?

turns.speaker: Jim Allister
turns.text: I repeat: Article 2 entrenches externally-made rights without democratic oversight. Dillon narrows its legal reach, but the political and constitutional problem remains; repeal of the Protocol is the proper remedy.
